newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's party boosted by East German activists.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's party boosted by East German activists.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl got a rare boost on Tuesday when seven former east German activists joined his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in protest against their own parties' wavering opposition to former communists.

The defections by the former dissidents had little effect on national politics because only Vera Lengsfeld, a Greens member who was spied on by her own husband and expelled to Britain in the 1980s, has a seat in the Bonn parliament.

But the news caused a sensation in eastern Germany, where defectors like Angelika Barbe and Guenter Nooke are known because they helped found the Social Democratic and Democratic Awakening parties in the dying days of East Germany.

The switch, warmly applauded by the centre-right coalition in Bonn, also marked the first success for Kohl's policy of wooing former eastern dissidents whose anti-communism has brought them closer to the CDU than the left-wing parties.

Baerbel Bohley, the best-known protest leader before the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989 and the most prominent target of Kohl's campaign, said the defections were a logical step but she had no intention herself of joining any political party.

Lengsfeld and Barbe accused the Greens and SPD of warming to the idea of local or state coalitions with the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successors to East Germany's communist party, after the next general election in 1998.

"We entered politics in 1989 with the goal of getting the Communist Party and its successor out of power," Lengsfeld told a news conference in Berlin. "The ominous rapproachement with the PDS is something that we cannot accept."

Kohl's CDU has stood alone in its unwavering condemnation of the PDS, which nearly vanished in 1990 but has rebounded to become the third strongest force in the east with an average 20 percent of the vote.
In some places like eastern Berlin, the PDS claims up to 40 percent support.

The SPD and Greens have ruled out an alliance in Bonn with the PDS but have been flirting with the PDS at the state and local level. The minority SPD-Green state government in Saxony-Anhalt depends on PDS support to survive.

The anti-communist easterners fear the PDS, which has styled itself a vocal defender of eastern Germans against west German "colonisation", could gain positions of power in the region after the next elections.
"The step by Vera Lengsfeld and other prominent civil rights leaders marks a triumph for the CDU," said CDU general secretary Peter Hintze at a news conference in Bonn.
"These leaders of the peaceful revolution against the Communist Party regime are saying that the CDU is the party that best represents the ideals of freedom."

Langsfeld discovered after German unification in 1990 that her husband Knut had been informing the hated Stasi security police about her dissident activities in the 1980s. She divorced him and dropped her married name Wollenberger.
Barbe, one of a handful of dissidents who revived the Social Democrats in East Germany even before the Wall fell, was a Bundestag deputy until 1994.

Nooke was Greens party leader in Brandenburg state, where he led a campaign against the popular premier Manfred Stolpe, who was accused of collaborating with the Stasi while he was a lawyer for the Protestant church in East Germany.

The other defectors were Ehrhart and Hildigund Neubert, who also helped found Democratic Awakening, a protest party that merged with the CDU in 1990. Its leader, former rebel pastor Reiner Eppelmann, is now head of the CDU's trade union wing.
The other two defectors were local civil rights activists Wolfgang Kupke and Markus Derling.
The Greens rejected Lengsfeld's charges and called on her to give up her seat in parliament. They also criticised her for strenghtening Kohl's fragile majority.
"I call on Vera Lengsfeld to return her Bundestag mandate," said the Greens leader Gunda Roestel. "It is a matter of political honesty and credibility."
